I've farmed this land in Quzhou for fifty years. My body knows the soil calendar. Here's how I think through this year:

**My land:** I rotate wheat and maize on about 7 mu — wheat goes in October, maize follows in June after I harvest the wheat. The remaining 3.1 mu I keep in chili. Chili brings in cash, so my wife and I tend it carefully.

**Wheat:** I'll plant the same improved variety I've used for years — Jimai or whatever the seed station is selling this season that most of my neighbors trust. I apply base fertilizer before planting, then top-dress nitrogen at jointing. I irrigate four times: before sowing to get good germination, once before winter sets in, again at jointing, and at heading. I spray herbicide in winter and again at the flag leaf stage for powdery mildew. My son is in the city, so I try to time heavier labor on weekends when grandchildren can help.

**Maize:** I go straight in after wheat harvest, no plowing — the soil is already loose and I'm racing the clock. I use hybrid seed, everyone does now. Three irrigations: one before planting, one at tasseling, one at grain fill. I'll spray once for corn borer. The combine does most of the work.

**Chili:** This is my main income crop. I transplant seedlings in late April. Chili drinks water, especially during flowering and fruit set, so I irrigate five or six times from my well. I apply more phosphorus and potassium here than on grain crops — chili needs it for fruit quality. Aphids and spider mites are my biggest headache, so I spray four times through the season. I plough deep before transplanting.
